newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tired Russia cosmonauts en route to Earth from Mir.
newsitem.headline: Tired Russia cosmonauts en route to Earth from Mir.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts left the stricken Mir space station on Thursday and headed for earth aboard a Soyuz spacecraft after one of the toughest assignments in the history of manned space flight.

Live television pictures at Mission Control outside the Russian capital showed Soyuz with commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin departing from Mir at 12:56 p.m. Moscow time (0856 GMT).
There appeared to be a three-minute delay in the operation compared to the original schedule but a Mission Control operator said the undocking went well.
"Everything is all right with you," the operator told the crew. "Thank God," replied Tsibliyev.

Along with British-born NASA astronaut Michael Foale, who will stay aboard Mir until next month, they have endured a series of major woes since they came aboard Mir in February. The most serious was a June 25 collision between the station and its supply ship.
Mir has run on partial power since then. They also had to contend with a fire and a series of problems with their life support systems during their mission.

Earlier on Thursday the pair embraced Foale and their two Russian replacements, commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, waved for the cameras as they floated into the airlock between Mir and Soyuz.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said in a live broadcast from Mir shown on television screens at Mission Control outside Moscow.
"We are leaving. See you on earth."
A Mission Control operator told Tsibliyev and Lazutkin: "Thank you for the job you've done. Happy landing."
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin are due to touch down at 1216 GMT in the ex-Soviet republic of Kazakhstan.

Despite the warm words from Mission Control on Thursday, Tsibliyev and Lazutkin face an uncertain reception on Earth. President Boris Yeltsin said last week human error may have been to blame for the June 25 crash, which threatened Mir's future.
But Yeltsin's space and aviation aide, Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov told Interfax news agency on Thursday no hasty conclusions should be drawn until a proper investigation into the accident.
It will also be hard for the returning cosmonauts not to be haunted by the past as they hurtle to Earth.
In 1971 the capsule carrying the three pioneers on Moscow's first space station Salyut touched down after a successful mission hailed throughout the then Soviet Union.
But when excited ground staff opened the hatch they found that all three men had died on the way down, killed by a sudden drop in pressure during re-entry into the earth's atmosphere.
Sixteen years later two cosmonauts undocked from the Mir space station which had replaced Salyut expecting a trouble-free return to earth.
They did land safely, but only after a nightmarish two days in what the Izvestia newspaper called "a lone boat drifting on a boundless ocean" after failing to align properly for re-entry.
But such incidents are the exception amid the many Soviet and then Russian space missions which followed Yuri Gagarin's pioneering flight into space in 1965.

Like the weary Mir crew, one of whom pulled out a plug on a computer by mistake while battling with the power problems, space officials have learnt from their mistakes. Special light spacesuits were introduced after the 1971 tragedy and they do not expect any big problems with Thursday's landing.

A fleet of helicopters will be on hand to track the capsule after a huge parachute opens to slow its fall once it enters earth's atmosphere. Rescue officials and mission control outside Moscow will also have radio contact with the craft.
After the June crash, Tsibliyev began suffering heart irregularities which doctors said were stress-related. A top medical adviser said he would need no special medicine for his Thursday return.
But Igor Goncharov, chief doctor of the mission, told reporters accompanying the rescue team in Kazakhstan:

"We have strengthened the team and taken on additional specialists -- a cardiologist from the military hospital and a doctor of intensive care. There could be unforseen situations, so we have taken these measures."
